events.title: Challenger is lost
events.description: Seven people die when the shuttle breaks apart after launch. NASA pauses flights and investigates.

events.title: Black Monday hits markets
events.description: The Dow falls 22.6% in one day. The monthly chart combines that day with all the other trading days in October.

events.title: The Berlin Wall opens
events.description: East Germans begin crossing the border freely. The change becomes a powerful symbol of a changing Europe.

what_happened_next.text:
Every choice finished higher over five years, with the international share basket leading this set. Colgate-Palmolive did best among the three individual companies. The toothpaste competition was easy to picture, but a useful new package was only one small part of a company's business.

The period included the Challenger disaster in 1986 and Black Monday in 1987. On that October day, the Dow fell 22.6%. The monthly chart does not show each daily swing, and a strong final gain does not remove the frightening losses that came first.

In November 1989, the Berlin Wall opened. This was a major change in people's lives and in Europe. It did not provide a simple rule for choosing among the seven investments.

Compare the results rather than looking only at the winner. The US share basket more than doubled, even though it finished behind the international basket. An investment can do well without coming first, and these dollar gains still need to be considered alongside rising prices.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Voters had re-elected Reagan, tax changes were being debated, and even toothpaste packaging was a business battleground.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The money grew through many monthly changes. Broad foreign shares led these choices, while owning one company brought its own separate risks.
reflection.what_faded_away: A new package or a movie opening did not reveal five years of returns. A memorable product story was not a complete investing plan.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: The market crash and the opening of the Berlin Wall were still ahead. Neither the smoothness of the journey nor the winner was known.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: Procter & Gamble bought Richardson-Vicks in 1985, expanding its health-care brands. Its everyday products also kept selling: profit for the year ending June 1989 rose 18%, helped by record US shipments and strong business abroad. Those growing sales and profits gave the investment’s rise a concrete business foundation.

Colgate-Palmolive reported higher annual earnings in 1986 as sales and new products did well. In 1987 it bought Softsoap, adding a familiar liquid-soap brand. The company was finding more products to sell alongside toothpaste and other household goods during a five-year stretch of strong investment gains.

GE completed its purchase of RCA in June 1986, bringing the NBC television network into the company. Its earnings also grew: 1988 profit reached about $3.4 billion, up 16% from 1987. GE’s strong investment result came as the business expanded beyond its familiar appliances and industrial equipment.
